quotes.verbatim_quote: a very effective type of learning takes place while watching television and noodling.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Validates informal, low-pressure practice as a legitimate learning mode, giving students permission to count passive playing time.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Sometimes it's helpful to sketch out a very simple melody line over the changes, i.e. half note, quarter notes, halves, etc. Let this line run through your head as a basic melody and play "fills" around it. This wil! at least get your line started with some form.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Provides a concrete structural entry point for building a solo line when the student is stuck.

quotes.verbatim_quote: A very common form for building a solo line is: QUESTION AND ANSWER. When this Q/A routine re-occurs, it is generally called a sequence.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Names and defines the Q/A sequence concept, which is a foundational structural principle for melodic improvisation.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Listen to the "pre-recorded changes" and sing the solo the wa'
quotes.why_load_bearing: Directs students to internalize melodic ideas vocally before executing them on the instrument, a core ear-to-hand principle.

quotes.verbatim_quote: In this program you will reach many moments in which you hate that "same old lick" you "always play". Be aware of this point in the tune and the next time around, do something else, no stops.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Teaches students to recognize and break habitual patterns in real time without interrupting the flow of improvisation.

quotes.verbatim_quote: HANGUPS: Play very slowly and listen carefully for any flams. Use all up strokes. Make each note sound as loud and strong as any other. Now use all up strokes, scales, interval skips. Now use consecutive down and up strokes. Now reverse to all up (on the down beat) and down (on the up beat) strokes.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Prescribes a specific diagnostic and corrective picking sequence for eliminating timing flams and uneven note dynamics.

quotes.verbatim_quote: At the beginning of each practice session, warm up for 5 minutes by playing notes all over the fingerboard. Play very slowly, low, high, and medium pitches, to develop a feel for string travel at a given picking area. Notes played high up on the neck have a much greater string travel than the low ones and can create coordination problems between the left and right hands. Both must attack the string simultaneously.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Explains why register-spanning warm-up matters mechanically — string travel distance varies by position and directly causes left/right-hand synchronization failures.

quotes.verbatim_quote: A most common mistake is to blame the left hand when the right hand is at fault, or vice versa. Watch out for this.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Warns against a universal misdiagnosis habit that causes students to practice the wrong hand and never fix the actual problem.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Get the progression off the paper and into your head as soon as possible. Memorizing the chord changes allows you to focus all of your attention on what you are playing rather than reading the music.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the direct cognitive reason for memorization: reading splits attention away from real-time musical decision-making.

quotes.verbatim_quote: The objectives put forth in this book are attainable only if the reader follows each step of the program without deviation from the schedule (that means no missed days, hours shortened, time frames disobeyed, key centers missed, introducing hammer-on's, pull-off's, before stated, playin tted eighth six- teenth notes instead of eighth notes, etc., etc.) If you do it, you get It. you don't, you don't.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes the method's non-negotiable contract with the student, specifying exact categories of deviation that will undermine results.

quotes.verbatim_quote: In the Growth Process, we all go through periods in which we are activating new nerve junctures, both in the brain and throughout other parts of the body. This type of growth work draws a tremendous amount of systemic energies. The overall physical feeling is like pulling a train uphill, and the psychological spin-off is the feeling that we are getting nowhere. This will persist for some period of time. We then tend to go into a natural state of rest, "a plateau." During this rest period, we tend to feel that we have the world by the tail and great progress is taking place. Actually the reverse is true. The progress was made during the uphill climb, not during the rest period.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Inverts students' intuitive reading of their own progress by explaining that subjective difficulty signals real growth while felt fluency signals a plateau, preventing them from mistaking struggle for failure.

quotes.verbatim_quote: So, on and on it goes, but your practice regimen must remain constant.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Delivers the actionable takeaway from the plateau discussion: the only correct response to the cycle is an unwavering schedule.
